text: Chapter Four Teaching Students with Autism No single method for teaching students with autism is successful for all students, and students' needs change over time. This chapter covers approaches that have proved successful, in five sections: instructional approaches, classroom management, communication development, social skills, and functional skills. Instructional approaches Visual approaches The  most strongly recommended approach  is to use visual aids. Students often show relative strengths in concrete thinking, rote memory, and visual-spatial understanding, and difficulties in abstract thinking, social cognition, communication, and attention. Pictographic and written cues can help the student learn, communicate, and develop self-control. Visual aids stay available for as long as the student needs to process the information.  Oral information is transient  — once said, it's gone — which is a problem for students who process language slowly or struggle to block out background stimulation. Visual aids range from concrete to abstract: Real object / situation → Facsimile → Colour photo → Colour picture → B&W picture → Line drawing → Graphic symbol → Written language Concrete Abstract Graphic symbols, though abstract, have been widely successful. To work, visual supports must  match the student's level of comprehension  — using a line drawing when the student needs colour photographs will only frustrate everyone. Visual supports can be used to: organize activity  — daily schedules, mini-schedules, activity checklists, calendars, choice boards give directions  — visual display of assignments, file cards with task directions, pictographs and written instructions clarify the environment  — labels on objects and containers, signs, lists, charts, messages support appropriate behaviour  — posted rules, visual steps of routines teach social skills  — illustrated social stories for specific situations teach self-control  — pictographs that cue behaviour expectations The key question When planning an activity or giving an instruction, ask:  how can this information be presented in a simple visual format?  Choose visual aids based on an understanding of the student and their abilities and responses. Provide precise, positive praise while the student is learning Tell students exactly what they did right: "great colouring," "good finishing of that math problem." Students with autism may learn in one trial, so direct praise to the specific behaviour: "Sal, you are doing very well at multiplying these numbers." Generalized praise risks  superstitious learning  — if you say "Sal, you are doing very well" while Sal is also swinging his feet, he may connect the foot swinging with the praise. Use meaningful reinforcements Reinforcers can be anything from praise to tangible objects that increase the target behaviour. Students with autism may not be motivated by common reinforcers. They might prefer time alone, talking to a preferred staff member, a trip to the cafeteria, a walk, time with a desired object, music, water play, a favourite routine, specific sensory items, or sitting at the window. Build a  "likes and dislikes" preference profile  with the family and share it with all service providers. Plan tasks at an appropriate level of difficulty Students may be especially vulnerable to anxiety and frustration when they can't perform a task. Increase difficulty gradually and scaffold learning — particularly with visual information rather than oral explanation alone. Use age-appropriate materials Honour the student's dignity: even if instruction is heavily modified, materials should suit the student's age. Provide opportunities for choice Much of these students' lives may be highly structured by adults, and some keep choosing one thing because they don't know how to choose another. Develop individual methods of offering choice and teach choosing directly.  Limit choice to one or two preferred activities  until the student grasps the concept — open-ended choices only frustrate. Break down oral instructions into small steps Avoid long strings of verbal information; support oral instruction with visual cues. Pay attention to processing and pacing Students may need longer to respond, due to cognitive and/or motor difficulties, and may need to process each piece of a message separately. Allow extra time generally, and  ample wait time  between instruction and response. Use concrete examples and hands-on activities Teach abstract ideas with specific examples, and vary the examples so the concept isn't accidentally learned as applying in only one way. Use task analysis Break complex tasks into sub-tasks and reinforce small, teachable steps. For example, brushing teeth becomes: get toothbrush and toothpaste → turn on water → wet toothbrush → unscrew toothpaste lid → put toothpaste on brush → … Life, social, and academic skills can all be taught this way, each step taught and then linked to the next in a chain. Use discrete trial methods Prompts may be physical, gestural, or verbal, and should be used only as long as needed — students can become dependent on them. In a discrete trial, the instructor presents the  stimulus  (instruction), gives a  prompt , the student  responds , and the instructor provides a  consequence  based on behavioural principles. Example objective:  Given an oral direction, Jackie will touch the card with the correct number when presented with cards numbered 1–5. Stimulus Instructor prompt Student response Consequence "Touch 5." Taps card #5 Touches card #5 ✓ Smiles, says "Good work, Jackie." "Touch 5." Points at card #5 Touches card #3 ✗ Turns head; no verbal response "Touch 5." Taps card #5 Flaps hands ✗ Turns head; no verbal response "Touch 5." Points at card #5 Touches card #5 ✓ Smiles, says "Good work, Jackie." Introduce unfamiliar tasks in a familiar environment when possible When that isn't possible, prepare the student for the new task and setting with pictures, videos, and/or social stories. Organize materials to highlight what is important Use organization aids and visual supports to help the student attend to pertinent information and learn new tasks. Remove extraneous materials from the desk before teaching; present only the text to be read rather than the whole book; highlight key words such as character names. Encourage independence and avoid prompt dependency Constantly supported students may never learn to act independently. Strategies include: using visual aids to reduce reliance on physical and verbal prompts planning ways to  fade prompts not always positioning the adult close to the student, and varying which adults are present (e.g., rotating teacher assistants) providing visual organizers — schedules, task outlines, checklists, charts — and involving the student in making them teaching awareness of environmental cues teaching in the environments containing the cues and reinforcement that will prompt and maintain the behaviour Direct and broaden fixations into useful activities If the student is fixated on an object or topic (a colour, a shape), use it to teach concepts. A whole week of writing and math can centre on one topic. Know the individual Keep a list of strengths and interests. Families can tell you what the student knows and does at home and in the community — build on these for instruction and reinforcement. Develop talent and interest areas If the student shows strength in an area (music, drama, art, graphics, computers), provide opportunities to develop expertise. This brings enjoyment and success, and may lead to future employment skills. Strategies for classroom management Provide a structured, predictable environment This is  not  an authoritarian approach. Structure provides consistency and clarity so students know where things belong, what is expected, and what comes next. Provide a customized visual daily schedule The student's schedule should fit within the class schedule. Vary tasks to prevent boredom; alternate familiar, successful activities with less preferred ones; alternate large-group activities with quiet calming time; build in physical activity throughout the day. Post the schedule at or near the student's desk. Teach the student to use it independently, and direct them to it at transition times. It can also make me so aware of what I feel that it is painful." — Donna Williams, an adult with autism,  Somebody Somewhere , 1994 Building a sensory inventory An inventory of sensory factors helps minimize their negative effect. Parents and others who know the student are valuable sources. Questions to consider: Auditory Fans, loudspeakers, fire alarms, several people talking, air conditioners, bells, barking, scraping? General sound level; predictability and repetitiveness of sounds? What can minimize their effect? Student's verbal comprehension and time needed to process and shift auditory attention. Visual Distracters — light, movement, reflection, background patterns? Student's eye level; teacher's position relative to student. Time required to shift visual attention. Reducing aversive visual stimuli helps behaviour and learning. Tactile Aversive textures? Appropriate temperatures? Does the student need to explore through touch, yet avoid being touched? Ability or defensiveness with instructional objects. Vestibular The student's need to move and exercise. Reactions to movement. How to build in movement without disrupting other students. Gustatory & olfactory Taste and smell preferences for foods and materials. Responses to smells of materials when choosing activities. Effects on teaching snack/mealtime behaviour. Note aspects of tasks that create frustration Look for problem areas that may cause sensory overload or frustration. Offer calming sensory experiences alongside potentially frustrating tasks. Adapt tasks and materials to promote success, and reduce environmental distracters and confusing or upsetting activities where feasible. Provide relaxation opportunities and areas A calm, quiet, designated area may be needed. For some students, relaxing means engaging in calming repetitive behaviours; students who crave movements like rocking can be given a time and place where this is permitted. Provide meaningful contact with peers who model appropriate behaviour Teach appropriate social behaviour and situation-specific expectations. Opportunities include: shared learning arrangements buddies for hallways, playground, and unstructured times varying buddies  across time and activities to prevent dependence on one child involving peers in individualized instruction cross-age buddies (an older student assists) pairing students at assemblies, clubs, and special events facilitating after-school and extracurricular involvement Plan for transitions and prepare the student for change Changes in activity, setting, or routine are often very stressful. Visual schedules help students understand and cooperate with changes; illustrated social stories prepare them for new situations. Strategies for communication development Expanding communication is one of the greatest challenges for teachers and families. Most children develop communication automatically by age three or four; many students with autism have not and must be taught. Helping them express wants and needs, interact socially, share information, express emotions, and protest or escape aversive situations is a  priority . Instruction may begin in structured settings, but  generalization requires natural settings  — functional language is best taught where it will be used. Opportunity alone isn't enough, though: target specific skills and strategies. The school team, parents, and specialists (especially the speech and language pathologist) should collaborate on goals. General suggestions: Focus on interaction and communication in the environments where the child participates (classroom, playground, gym). Use sentences — you're modelling speech as well as communicating. Use vocabulary matched to comprehension; for more severe disability, choose familiar, specific, concrete words and repeat as needed. Use  clear, simple, concise  language. Figures of speech, irony, and sarcasm confuse. Allow processing time  — talk more slowly or pause between words as needed. "Autism…stops me from finding and using my own words when I want to. Or makes me use all the words and silly things I do not want to say." — Donna Williams,  Somebody Somewhere , 1994 Learning to listen Students often need structured lessons on listening. Break listening into components — face the speaker, look at one spot (not necessarily eye contact), place hands in a planned position — and praise or reward each step. Developing oral language comprehension Pair spoken language with objects, pictures, and photographs to gain attention and aid comprehension. Interestingly, many students with autism use  reading to support oral comprehension  rather than the reverse, making reading instruction especially significant. With higher-functioning students, don't assume understanding just because they can repeat information —  check for comprehension . Developing oral language expression Most students develop some form of communication, even if not traditional speech. Know the student's form of expression and adjust expectations; for students with limited speech,  accept limited verbal attempts and non-verbal behaviour as communicative . A customized  communication dictionary  documents what the student says, what it means, and planned adult responses. Teach new vocabulary in varied contexts with a visual approach. Students need to learn that: everything in our world has a name there are different ways of saying the same thing words can be meaningful in a variety of contexts using words helps them communicate their needs and desires Students who use pictures need to learn that a picture has a name and can give direction. Include situations that encourage: requests  — for food, toys, or help negation  — refusing, protesting, or indicating they want to stop commenting  — labelling pictures or objects, greetings, play Developing conversation skills Virtually all people with autism struggle with pragmatics — even those with good vocabulary. Provide structured play built around the student's interests, using modelling, physical prompts, visual cues, and reinforcement. Simple drawings (e.g.,  Comic Strip Conversations ) can show what people say, do, and think, with symbols for listening, interrupting, loud and quiet words, talk and thoughts; colours can represent emotions. Scripts help with specific situations. Give  concrete rules  in a visual format, and provide real social and community experiences to practise. Echolalia Echolalia — literal repetition of others' words — is part of normal early language development, but some learners with autism seem to stop developing at this level. It can be  immediate  or  delayed  (even months or years later). Immediate echolalia  can be a teaching tool: when a student echoes back a question, model the appropriate response and reinforce it when the student echoes that. Consult the SLP for individual strategies. Delayed echolalia  (e.g., repeating TV commercials word for word) can be thought of as a stored chunk of language triggered by a situation or emotion. Don't assume the student understands its content. Try to identify the trigger and prompt appropriate language — e.g., a student reciting a soft-drink ad turned out to be thirsty; the teacher tested this with "You feel thirsty and want a drink?" Sometimes no logical connection is ever found. Alternative or augmentative communication (AAC) An augmentative system is any approach that supports, enhances, or adds to how a person communicates — for non-verbal students or those who can't use speech functionally. Systems range from low-tech (no power) to high-tech. Alternative communication may include: direct movement of a person or object (pulling a teacher to the door to go outside) gestures or body actions (shaking the head) real objects (bringing a jacket to ask to go home) picture representations (e.g., the  Picture Exchange Communication System, PECS ) voice without conventional words ("Ah-ah-ah" for the toilet) written messages, pointed to or typed sign language (e.g., ASL or Signed English) Choosing a system should be based on assessment of cognitive ability, skills, interests, and motor abilities. The options form a continuum: Full-sized objects → Miniature objects → Gestures → Photographs → Drawings → Written words → Written phrases → Written sentences → Signing Concrete Highly abstract Parents are key: the system must be used at home and school to be effective. The SLP or another AAC specialist can help decide; the teacher often implements it. Computer-based communication and learning show promising results. Strategies for teaching social skills Most students with autism  want to be part of the social world , but haven't automatically learned the unwritten rules. Many operate on rigid, overly literal misperceptions: rules apply in only a single situation everything someone says must be true when you don't know what to do, do nothing Never assume a student with autism understands a situation or social expectation. They may use an ineffective method because they don't know a better one, or can't distinguish between situations. Assess social competencies to determine which skills to teach directly. Integrated environments provide peer models and natural cues, but access alone is usually not enough —  explicit teaching is needed . Using social stories Developed by Carol Gray, a  social story  describes a social situation — including social cues and appropriate responses — written for a specific situation and student. Uses include: facilitating inclusion in regular classes introducing changes and new routines explaining others' behaviour teaching situation-specific social skills teaching new academic skills A social story should describe the situation  from the student's perspective , direct the appropriate behaviour, and be written in the student's voice ("I"). The author observes the situation, considers what the student sees, hears, and feels, then writes at the right comprehension level using three sentence types: Descriptive  — the setting, activity, and people involved Directive  — positive statements of the desired response Perspective  — possible reactions of others Rule of thumb: 2–5 descriptive statements + 1 directive statement = social story Best format: a booklet with one or two sentences per page and one main concept per page. Example: My Turn on the Computer p.1 If I wait for my turn on the computer, the other kids like me better. p.2 Everyone likes to have a turn on the computer. p.3 When other kids are using the computer, I will be quiet and wait for my turn. p.4 When I am finished on the computer, other kids can use it. That is okay, because I know I can use it the next day. p.5 When I wait for my turn on the computer, everyone will be happy. Three ways to implement a social story: Independent reader:  an adult reads it twice, the student reads it back, then reads it daily. Non-reader:  record it with a signal (e.g., a bell) to turn pages; the student "reads" it daily. Add symbols, drawings, or photos. Modelling:  videotape the story read aloud, one page on screen at a time. Teaching key social rules Understanding basic rules for a situation helps the child adapt, may reduce anxiety, and reduces reliance on inappropriate coping behaviours. Critical skills that usually need direct instruction: Skill How to teach it Waiting Visual cues (object, pictures, written words) make waiting less abstract and more situation-specific. Taking turns Social stories, a picture/pictograph cue, plus instruction and rehearsal in turn-taking activities. Transitions Social stories and warnings with visual cues. Prepare the student for possibly finishing an activity later. Changing the topic For perseveration: visual rules, time limits, and a set time and place for the favourite topic. Finishing Teach use of environmental cues (watch what other children do); use a timer and a self-check method. Initiating Social stories with photos/pictures to teach approaching others, asking, joining a game, saying hello, and leaving if upset. Being flexible Show changes concretely — remove or cross out a picture in the schedule and put another in its place. Being quiet Visual supports for specific quiet behaviours and rules for specific situations. Using Cognitive Picture Rehearsal Present a sequence of behaviours as pictures or pictographs with a script, and guide the student through repeated practice of the sequence. Using peer support Educate peers first so they understand the student's behaviour — interpret non-verbal communication, explain what's hard, and show how to help. Young children can learn prompts to start and maintain interaction.  Reinforce peers  for their role too. Pivotal Response Training (PRT) , used at recess, has increased interaction, initiation, varied toy play, and language use. PRT teaches typical peers to: gain attention give choices to maintain motivation vary toys model social behaviour reinforce attempts encourage conversation extend conversation take turns narrate play Parents should be involved in any decision to discuss autism with their child's peers; they may wish to preview materials or help present. Using social skills training groups Small, structured groups can help. Good programs start with an assessment, and lessons follow a common format: Identify the skill, its components, and when it's used Model the skill Role play Practise Use strategies for generalization These curricula weren't designed for autism, so adapt them and put extra emphasis on generalization. Integrated play groups For younger students, play groups with age peers create natural situations to express wants, practise being near other children, and imitate social interactions. Teaching self-monitoring / self-management For higher-functioning students, self-management — monitoring one's own behaviour to earn reinforcement — increases independence. Simply collecting self-monitoring data tends to increase the desired behaviour; accuracy matters less than the awareness it builds. Define the target behaviour the student will self-monitor. Identify reinforcers that work for the individual. Create a self-monitoring method (a chart, stickers, a low-tech counter). Teach the target behaviour and how to record it. Gradually reduce adult intervention so the student self-manages. Supporting the development of friendships Students with basic social skills may still struggle to connect with and maintain relationships with peers. Teachers and parents can help by: encouraging a friend to play with the child at home helping the student join school clubs, with support teaching the child to observe other children to know what to do encouraging co-operative games modelling how to relate to the child and educating classmates encouraging prospective friendships making break times enjoyable projects that illustrate the qualities of a good friend directly teaching how to read faces and body language and respond to emotional cues Teaching functional skills A fundamental goal of schooling is independent functioning — especially important for students with autism. Functional skill goals should be in the student's IEP, taught with the same strategies used elsewhere. Functional skills span five domains: Self-care Hygiene, grooming, dressing, toileting (often needs significant planning), meal planning and food prep, eating, laundry, cleaning, handling money and budgeting (older students). Functional academics Communicating personal info (name, birth date, address, phone); reading signs and labels; measurement, counting, calendars, telling time. Vocational punctuality and reliable attendance following a job routine; completing duties understanding task completion following safety procedures accepting direction and correction responding appropriately to authority completing a cleanup routine appropriate work attire and grooming using breaks and lunch appropriately Leisure Team and individual sports, arts, performances, nature activities, organized groups, social events. At home: using TV/stereo, caring for pets, card games, crafts. Participation may be full or partial. Community Safety is a major concern.  Consider: public transit; finding pools, rec centres, banks; pedestrian rules and traffic; public washrooms; restaurant skills like ordering food. Schools and families should coordinate so instruction is consistent. Some skills involve very personal areas of life, so plan with sensitivity and care. Summary of suggestions for teaching students with autism Use visual methods post daily schedules individualized mini-schedules activity checklists choice boards label objects and containers post illustrated classroom rules visual steps for routines visual cues to support oral directions Additional teaching approaches break tasks into components behaviour-specific praise effective reinforcers discrete trial strategies behaviour-shaping strategies appropriate difficulty level age-appropriate materials opportunities for choice simple oral instructions + visuals pace to the student's level allow processing time; wait patiently use interests to motivate highlight important information Classroom management structured, predictable environment customized schedule at student's desk remove stimuli that trigger problem behaviour minimize effects of stimuli that can't be removed adapt tasks to avoid frustration provide a relaxation area contact with peers who model routines plan transitions carefully Communication Listening:  structured lessons; reinforce each component Comprehension:  visual aids, gestures, written language with speech Expression:  reinforce attempts; teach vocabulary visually; everything has a name; use desired items to prompt; elicit comments Conversation:  modelling; structured play; discuss routines; link behaviours and thoughts; scripts; rules for social discourse Social skills social stories teach components of key skills planned practice and reinforcement cognitive picture rehearsal peer support social skills training groups support friendships
